raw: CHAPTER XIV. The Knitting Done
en: [Chapter 14] The Knitting Done

raw: In that same juncture of time when the Fifty-Two awaited their fate Madame Defarge held darkly ominous council with The Vengeance and Jacques Three of the Revolutionary Jury.
en: At the exact same time the fifty-two prisoners waited for their deaths, Madame Defarge held a dark meeting with The Vengeance and Jacques Three of the Revolutionary Jury.

raw: Not in the wine-shop did Madame Defarge confer with these ministers, but in the shed of the wood-sawyer, erst a mender of roads.
en: She did not meet with these helpers in her wine-shop, but in the shed of the wood-sawyer, who used to be a road repairer.

raw: The sawyer himself did not participate in the conference, but abided at a little distance, like an outer satellite who was not to speak until required, or to offer an opinion until invited.
en: The wood-sawyer himself did not take part in the meeting. He stood a short distance away, like a servant waiting to be told when to speak or give an opinion.

raw: “But our Defarge,” said Jacques Three, “is undoubtedly a good Republican? Eh?”
en: “But our Defarge,” said Jacques Three, “is definitely a good Republican, isn't he?”

raw: “There is no better,” the voluble Vengeance protested in her shrill notes, “in France.”
en: “There is no better in all of France,” the talkative Vengeance declared in her high, squeaky voice.

raw: “Peace, little Vengeance,” said Madame Defarge, laying her hand with a slight frown on her lieutenant’s lips, “hear me speak.
en: “Quiet, little Vengeance,” said Madame Defarge, putting her hand over her helper's mouth with a slight frown. “Listen to me speak.

raw: My husband, fellow-citizen, is a good Republican and a bold man; he has deserved well of the Republic, and possesses its confidence.
en: My husband, fellow citizen, is a good Republican and a brave man. He has served the Republic well and has its trust.

raw: But my husband has his weaknesses, and he is so weak as to relent towards this Doctor.”
en: But my husband has his weaknesses, and he is weak enough to feel pity for this Doctor.”

raw: “It is a great pity,” croaked Jacques Three, dubiously shaking his head, with his cruel fingers at his hungry mouth; “it is not quite like a good citizen; it is a thing to regret.”
en: “That is a great pity,” croaked Jacques Three, shaking his head doubtfully while biting his twitching fingers. “That is not like a good citizen; it is very regrettable.”

raw: “See you,” said madame, “I care nothing for this Doctor, I.
en: “Listen,” Madame Defarge said, “I don't care about this Doctor at all.

raw: He may wear his head or lose it, for any interest I have in him; it is all one to me.
en: He can keep his head or lose it for all I care; it makes no difference to me.

raw: But, the Evrémonde people are to be exterminated, and the wife and child must follow the husband and father.”
en: But the Evrémonde family must be wiped out, and the wife and child must follow the husband and father to the Guillotine.”

raw: “She has a fine head for it,” croaked Jacques Three. “I have seen blue eyes and golden hair there, and they looked charming when Samson held them up.” Ogre that he was, he spoke like an epicure.
en: “She has a beautiful head for it,” croaked Jacques Three. “I have seen blue eyes and golden hair on the platform before, and they looked lovely when Samson the executioner held them up.” Monster that he was, he spoke like a man describing a delicious meal.

raw: Madame Defarge cast down her eyes, and reflected a little.
en: Madame Defarge looked down, thinking for a moment.

raw: “The child also,” observed Jacques Three, with a meditative enjoyment of his words, “has golden hair and blue eyes.
en: “The child also,” Jacques Three noted with calm enjoyment, “has golden hair and blue eyes.

raw: And we seldom have a child there.
en: And we rarely have children on the platform.

raw: It is a pretty sight!”
en: It is a pretty sight!”

raw: “In a word,” said Madame Defarge, coming out of her short abstraction, “I cannot trust my husband in this matter.
en: “In short,” Madame Defarge said, snapping out of her thoughts, “I cannot trust my husband in this matter.

raw: Not only do I feel, since last night, that I dare not confide to him the details of my projects; but also I feel that if I delay, there is danger of his giving warning, and then they might escape.”
en: Since last night, I feel that I cannot tell him the details of my plans. I also know that if I wait, he might warn them, and they might escape.”

raw: “That must never be,” croaked Jacques Three; “no one must escape.
en: “That must never happen,” croaked Jacques Three. “No one must escape.

raw: We have not half enough as it is.
en: We don't have half enough executions as it is.

raw: We ought to have six score a day.”
en: We should have a hundred and twenty a day.”

raw: “In a word,” Madame Defarge went on, “my husband has not my reason for pursuing this family to annihilation, and I have not his reason for regarding this Doctor with any sensibility.
en: “In a word,” Madame Defarge continued, “my husband does not have my personal reason for wanting to destroy this family completely, and I don't have his reason for feeling sympathy for this Doctor.

raw: I must act for myself, therefore.
en: Therefore, I must act on my own.

raw: Come hither, little citizen.”
en: Come here, little citizen.”

raw: The wood-sawyer, who held her in the respect, and himself in the submission, of mortal fear, advanced with his hand to his red cap.
en: The wood-sawyer, who feared her with a deadly terror, stepped forward, touching his red cap respectfully.

raw: “Touching those signals, little citizen,” said Madame Defarge, sternly, “that she made to the prisoners; you are ready to bear witness to them this very day?”
en: “About those signals, little citizen,” Madame Defarge said sternly, “the ones she made to the prisoners; are you ready to testify about them today?”

raw: “Ay, ay, why not!” cried the sawyer. “Every day, in all weathers, from two to four, always signalling, sometimes with the little one, sometimes without.
en: “Yes, yes, why not!” cried the sawyer. “Every day, in all kinds of weather, from two to four o'clock, she was always signaling, sometimes with the child, sometimes without.

raw: I know what I know.
en: I know what I know.

raw: I have seen with my eyes.”
en: I saw it with my own eyes.”

raw: He made all manner of gestures while he spoke, as if in incidental imitation of some few of the great diversity of signals that he had never seen.
en: He waved his hands around as he spoke, pretending to copy the signals that he had never actually seen.

raw: “Clearly plots,” said Jacques Three. “Transparently!”
en: “Clearly plotting,” said Jacques Three. “It is obvious!”

raw: “There is no doubt of the Jury?” inquired Madame Defarge, letting her eyes turn to him with a gloomy smile.
en: “Are you sure about the Jury?” Madame Defarge asked, looking at him with a dark smile.

raw: “Rely upon the patriotic Jury, dear citizeness.
en: “Trust the patriotic Jury, dear citizenness.

raw: I answer for my fellow-Jurymen.”
en: I will answer for my fellow jurors.”

raw: “Now, let me see,” said Madame Defarge, pondering again. “Yet once more!
en: “Now let me think,” said Madame Defarge, pondering again. “One more thing!

raw: Can I spare this Doctor to my husband?
en: Can I spare this Doctor for my husband's sake?

raw: I have no feeling either way.
en: I don't care either way.

raw: Can I spare him?”
en: Can I spare him?”

raw: “He would count as one head,” observed Jacques Three, in a low voice. “We really have not heads enough; it would be a pity, I think.”
en: “He would count as one more head,” Jacques Three noted in a low voice. “We really don't have enough heads; it would be a pity to lose him, I think.”

raw: “He was signalling with her when I saw her,” argued Madame Defarge; “I cannot speak of one without the other; and I must not be silent, and trust the case wholly to him, this little citizen here.
en: “He was signaling with her when I saw her,” Madame Defarge argued. “I cannot accuse one without the other. I must not stay silent and trust this case completely to this little citizen here.

raw: For, I am not a bad witness.”
en: After all, I am a very good witness.”

raw: The Vengeance and Jacques Three vied with each other in their fervent protestations that she was the most admirable and marvellous of witnesses.
en: The Vengeance and Jacques Three competed with each other to praise her, declaring she was the most wonderful and marvelous witness.

raw: The little citizen, not to be outdone, declared her to be a celestial witness.
en: The wood-sawyer, not wanting to be left out, declared she was a witness sent from heaven.

raw: “He must take his chance,” said Madame Defarge. “No, I cannot spare him!
en: “He must take his chances,” said Madame Defarge. “No, I cannot spare him!

raw: You are engaged at three o’clock; you are going to see the batch of to-day executed.--You?”
en: You are busy at three o'clock; you are going to watch today's executions, aren't you?”

raw: The question was addressed to the wood-sawyer, who hurriedly replied in the affirmative: seizing the occasion to add that he was the most ardent of Republicans, and that he would be in effect the most desolate of Republicans, if anything prevented him from enjoying the pleasure of smoking his afternoon pipe in the contemplation of the droll national barber.
en: The question was asked of the wood-sawyer, who quickly answered yes. He took the opportunity to add that he was the most passionate of Republicans, and that he would be the most miserable man in France if anything stopped him from enjoying his afternoon pipe while watching the Guillotine.

raw: He was so very demonstrative herein, that he might have been suspected (perhaps was, by the dark eyes that looked contemptuously at him out of Madame Defarge’s head) of having his small individual fears for his own personal safety, every hour in the day.
en: He was so dramatic about it that one might suspect, and Madame Defarge probably did, looking at him with scorn, that he lived in constant fear for his own head every hour of the day.

raw: “I,” said madame, “am equally engaged at the same place. After it is over--say at eight to-night--come you to me, in Saint Antoine, and we will give information against these people at my Section.”
en: “I will be at the same place,” Madame Defarge said. “After it is over, let's say at eight o'clock tonight, come to my house in Saint Antoine, and we will report these people to my revolutionary committee.”

raw: The wood-sawyer said he would be proud and flattered to attend the citizeness.
en: The wood-sawyer said he would be proud and honored to help the citizenness.

raw: The citizeness looking at him, he became embarrassed, evaded her glance as a small dog would have done, retreated among his wood, and hid his confusion over the handle of his saw.
en: When she stared at him, he became embarrassed. He looked away like a frightened dog, backed up into his pile of wood, and hid his confusion by working on his saw handle.

raw: Madame Defarge beckoned the Juryman and The Vengeance a little nearer to the door, and there expounded her further views to them thus:
en: Madame Defarge beckoned the juror and The Vengeance closer to the door, explaining the rest of her plan:

raw: “She will now be at home, awaiting the moment of his death.
en: “She will be at home now, waiting for the moment of his death.

raw: She will be mourning and grieving.
en: She will be crying and grieving.

raw: She will be in a state of mind to impeach the justice of the Republic.
en: She will be in a state of mind to insult the justice of the Republic.

raw: She will be full of sympathy with its enemies.
en: She will be full of sympathy for its enemies.

raw: I will go to her.”
en: I will go visit her.”

raw: “What an admirable woman; what an adorable woman!” exclaimed Jacques Three, rapturously. “Ah, my cherished!” cried The Vengeance; and embraced her.
en: “What a wonderful woman! What an amazing woman!” Jacques Three cried in delight. “Ah, my darling!” cried The Vengeance, hugging her.

raw: “Take you my knitting,” said Madame Defarge, placing it in her lieutenant’s hands, “and have it ready for me in my usual seat.
en: “Take my knitting,” said Madame Defarge, putting it in her assistant's hands, “and have it ready for me in my usual seat.

raw: Keep me my usual chair.
en: Save my usual chair.

raw: Go you there, straight, for there will probably be a greater concourse than usual, to-day.”
en: Go straight there, because there will probably be a larger crowd than usual today.”

raw: “I willingly obey the orders of my Chief,” said The Vengeance with alacrity, and kissing her cheek. “You will not be late?”
en: “I happily obey the orders of my leader,” said The Vengeance quickly, kissing her cheek. “You won't be late?”

raw: “I shall be there before the commencement.”
en: “I will be there before it starts.”

raw: “And before the tumbrils arrive.
en: “And before the death carts arrive.

raw: Be sure you are there, my soul,” said The Vengeance, calling after her, for she had already turned into the street, “before the tumbrils arrive!”
en: Be sure you are there, my dear,” The Vengeance called after her, as Madame Defarge had already turned into the street, “before the carts arrive!”

raw: Madame Defarge slightly waved her hand, to imply that she heard, and might be relied upon to arrive in good time, and so went through the mud, and round the corner of the prison wall.
en: Madame Defarge waved her hand slightly to show she heard and could be trusted to arrive on time. She walked through the mud and around the corner of the prison wall.

raw: The Vengeance and the Juryman, looking after her as she walked away, were highly appreciative of her fine figure, and her superb moral endowments.
en: The Vengeance and the juror watched her go, highly admiring her strong figure and her great revolutionary spirit.

raw: There were many women at that time, upon whom the time laid a dreadfully disfiguring hand; but, there was not one among them more to be dreaded than this ruthless woman, now taking her way along the streets.
en: There were many women in those days who had been made cruel by the hard times, but none was more feared than this ruthless woman walking down the streets.

raw: Of a strong and fearless character, of shrewd sense and readiness, of great determination, of that kind of beauty which not only seems to impart to its possessor firmness and animosity, but to strike into others an instinctive recognition of those qualities; the troubled time would have heaved her up, under any circumstances.
en: Strong, fearless, sharp-minded, and determined, she had a kind of beauty that showed her hatred and forced others to recognize her strength. The troubled times would have made her a leader under any circumstances.

raw: But, imbued from her childhood with a brooding sense of wrong, and an inveterate hatred of a class, opportunity had developed her into a tigress.
en: But since she had been filled since childhood with a deep sense of wrong and a hatred for the rich class, this opportunity had turned her into a tigress.

raw: She was absolutely without pity.
en: She was absolutely without pity.

raw: If she had ever had the virtue in her, it had quite gone out of her.
en: If she had ever possessed any kindness, it had completely vanished.

raw: It was nothing to her, that an innocent man was to die for the sins of his forefathers; she saw, not him, but them.
en: It meant nothing to her that an innocent man was going to die for the sins of his ancestors; she did not see him, but only his family name.

raw: It was nothing to her, that his wife was to be made a widow and his daughter an orphan; that was insufficient punishment, because they were her natural enemies and her prey, and as such had no right to live.
en: It meant nothing to her that his wife would be made a widow and his daughter an orphan; that was not enough punishment, because they were her natural enemies and her prey, and they had no right to live.

raw: To appeal to her, was made hopeless by her having no sense of pity, even for herself.
en: Begging her for mercy was useless because she felt no pity, not even for herself.

raw: If she had been laid low in the streets, in any of the many encounters in which she had been engaged, she would not have pitied herself; nor, if she had been ordered to the axe to-morrow, would she have gone to it with any softer feeling than a fierce desire to change places with the man who sent her there.
en: If she had been killed in the streets during the many fights she had been in, she would not have felt sorry for herself. If she were sentenced to die tomorrow, she would go to the Guillotine without any soft feelings, only a fierce desire to swap places with the judge who sent her there.

raw: Such a heart Madame Defarge carried under her rough robe.
en: Madame Defarge carried this hard heart under her rough dress.

raw: Carelessly worn, it was a becoming robe enough, in a certain weird way, and her dark hair looked rich under her coarse red cap.
en: Worn carelessly, it was a nice enough outfit in a strange way, and her dark hair looked rich under her coarse red cap.

raw: Lying hidden in her bosom, was a loaded pistol.
en: Hidden in her shirt was a loaded pistol.

raw: Lying hidden at her waist, was a sharpened dagger.
en: Hidden at her waist was a sharp dagger.

raw: Thus accoutred, and walking with the confident tread of such a character, and with the supple freedom of a woman who had habitually walked in her girlhood, bare-foot and bare-legged, on the brown sea-sand, Madame Defarge took her way along the streets.
en: Armed like this, walking with the confident step of a strong character and the easy movement of a woman who had walked barefoot on the beach as a girl, Madame Defarge went down the streets.

raw: Now, when the journey of the travelling coach, at that very moment waiting for the completion of its load, had been planned out last night, the difficulty of taking Miss Pross in it had much engaged Mr.
en: When the journey of the escape carriage, which was currently waiting for the family to get in, had been planned the night before, Mr.

raw: Lorry’s attention.
en: Lorry had worried about how to include Miss Pross.

raw: It was not merely desirable to avoid overloading the coach, but it was of the highest importance that the time occupied in examining it and its passengers, should be reduced to the utmost; since their escape might depend on the saving of only a few seconds here and there.
en: It was not just about avoiding an overloaded carriage, but it was crucial to minimize the time spent at checking stations, since their survival might depend on saving just a few seconds.

raw: Finally, he had proposed, after anxious consideration, that Miss Pross and Jerry, who were at liberty to leave the city, should leave it at three o’clock in the lightest-wheeled conveyance known to that period.
en: Finally, after careful thought, he suggested that Miss Pross and Jerry Cruncher, who were free to leave the city legally, should leave at three o'clock in a small, fast light carriage.

raw: Unencumbered with luggage, they would soon overtake the coach, and, passing it and preceding it on the road, would order its horses in advance, and greatly facilitate its progress during the precious hours of the night, when delay was the most to be dreaded.
en: Carrying no luggage, they would quickly catch up to the escape coach. They could then drive ahead of it, ordering fresh horses in advance at each station to speed up the journey during the dangerous hours of the night.

raw: Seeing in this arrangement the hope of rendering real service in that pressing emergency, Miss Pross hailed it with joy.
en: Seeing that this plan would really help in the emergency, Miss Pross agreed happily.

raw: She and Jerry had beheld the coach start, had known who it was that Solomon brought, had passed some ten minutes in tortures of suspense, and were now concluding their arrangements to follow the coach, even as Madame Defarge, taking her way through the streets, now drew nearer and nearer to the else-deserted lodging in which they held their consultation.
en: She and Jerry had watched the carriage leave and knew who Solomon was carrying. They had spent ten agonizing minutes waiting in suspense, and were now finishing their plans to follow the carriage, even as Madame Defarge walked through the streets, drawing closer and closer to the apartment where they were talking.

raw: “Now what do you think, Mr.
en: “Now, what do you think, Mr.

raw: Cruncher,” said Miss Pross, whose agitation was so great that she could hardly speak, or stand, or move, or live: “what do you think of our not starting from this courtyard?
en: Cruncher?” said Miss Pross, who was so nervous she could barely speak, stand, or move. “What do you think about us not leaving from this courtyard?

raw: Another carriage having already gone from here to-day, it might awaken suspicion.”
en: Since one carriage has already left this place today, another might make people suspicious.”

raw: “My opinion, miss,” returned Mr.
en: “My opinion, miss,” Mr.

raw: Cruncher, “is as you’re right.
en: Cruncher replied, “is that you're right.

raw: Likewise wot I’ll stand by you, right or wrong.”
en: And I will stand by you, right or wrong.”

raw: “I am so distracted with fear and hope for our precious creatures,” said Miss Pross, wildly crying, “that I am incapable of forming any plan.
en: “I am so distracted with fear and hope for our dear family,” said Miss Pross, crying wildly, “that I cannot think of any plan.

raw: Are _you_ capable of forming any plan, my dear good Mr.
en: Are _you_ able to make a plan, my dear, good Mr.

raw: Cruncher?”
en: Cruncher?”

raw: “Respectin’ a future spear o’ life, miss,” returned Mr.
en: “About my future way of life, miss,” Mr.

raw: Cruncher, “I hope so.
en: Cruncher replied, “I hope so.

raw: Respectin’ any present use o’ this here blessed old head o’ mine, I think not.
en: But as for using this brain of mine right now, I don't think I can.

raw: Would you do me the favour, miss, to take notice o’ two promises and wows wot it is my wishes fur to record in this here crisis?”
en: Would you do me a favor, miss, and listen to two promises and vows I want to make in this crisis?”

raw: “Oh, for gracious sake!” cried Miss Pross, still wildly crying, “record them at once, and get them out of the way, like an excellent man.”
en: “Oh, for goodness' sake!” cried Miss Pross, still crying. “Make them at once and get them out of the way, like a good man.”

raw: “First,” said Mr.
en: “First,” said Mr.

raw: Cruncher, who was all in a tremble, and who spoke with an ashy and solemn visage, “them poor things well out o’ this, never no more will I do it, never no more!”
en: Cruncher, shaking all over and looking pale and serious, “once those poor people are safely out of this, I will never dig up graves again, never again!”

raw: “I am quite sure, Mr.
en: “I am quite sure, Mr.

raw: Cruncher,” returned Miss Pross, “that you never will do it again, whatever it is, and I beg you not to think it necessary to mention more particularly what it is.”
en: Cruncher,” Miss Pross replied, “that you will never do it again, whatever it is, and I ask you not to mention the details of what it is.”

raw: “No, miss,” returned Jerry, “it shall not be named to you.
en: “No, miss,” Jerry replied, “I won't name it.

raw: Second: them poor things well out o’ this, and never no more will I interfere with Mrs.
en: Second: once those poor people are safe, I will never again yell at Mrs.

raw: Cruncher’s flopping, never no more!”
en: Cruncher for praying, never again!”

raw: “Whatever housekeeping arrangement that may be,” said Miss Pross, striving to dry her eyes and compose herself, “I have no doubt it is best that Mrs.
en: “Whatever religious arrangement that is,” said Miss Pross, trying to dry her eyes and calm down, “I'm sure it's best that Mrs.

raw: Cruncher should have it entirely under her own superintendence.--O my poor darlings!”
en: Cruncher manages it herself. Oh, my poor darlings!”

raw: “I go so far as to say, miss, moreover,” proceeded Mr.
en: “I will even go so far as to say, miss,” Mr.

raw: Cruncher, with a most alarming tendency to hold forth as from a pulpit--“and let my words be took down and took to Mrs.
en: Cruncher continued, speaking like a preacher in a church, “and let my words be passed on to Mrs.

raw: Cruncher through yourself--that wot my opinions respectin’ flopping has undergone a change, and that wot I only hope with all my heart as Mrs.
en: Cruncher by you, that my opinions about praying have completely changed, and I hope with all my heart that Mrs.

raw: Cruncher may be a flopping at the present time.”
en: Cruncher is praying right now.”

raw: “There, there, there!
en: “There, there!

raw: I hope she is, my dear man,” cried the distracted Miss Pross, “and I hope she finds it answering her expectations.”
en: I hope she is, my dear man,” cried the worried Miss Pross, “and I hope it brings her what she hopes for.”

raw: “Forbid it,” proceeded Mr.
en: “God forbid,” Mr.

raw: Cruncher, with additional solemnity, additional slowness, and additional tendency to hold forth and hold out, “as anything wot I have ever said or done should be wisited on my earnest wishes for them poor creeturs now!
en: Cruncher went on, even more slowly and solemnly, “that anything I have said or done in the past should hurt my wishes for those poor people now!

raw: Forbid it as we shouldn’t all flop (if it was anyways conwenient) to get ’em out o’ this here dismal risk!
en: God forbid that we shouldn't all pray, if it helped, to get them out of this terrible danger!

raw: Forbid it, miss!
en: God forbid, miss!

raw: Wot I say, for-_bid_ it!” This was Mr.
en: That is what I say: God forbid it!” This was Mr.

raw: Cruncher’s conclusion after a protracted but vain endeavour to find a better one.
en: Cruncher's final statement after trying hard to find a better way to say it.

raw: And still Madame Defarge, pursuing her way along the streets, came nearer and nearer.
en: And still Madame Defarge walked down the streets, coming closer and closer.

raw: “If we ever get back to our native land,” said Miss Pross, “you may rely upon my telling Mrs.
en: “If we ever get back to England,” Miss Pross said, “you can count on me to tell Mrs.

raw: Cruncher as much as I may be able to remember and understand of what you have so impressively said; and at all events you may be sure that I shall bear witness to your being thoroughly in earnest at this dreadful time.
en: Cruncher as much of this as I can remember. In any case, I will testify that you were completely sincere during this terrible time.

raw: Now, pray let us think!
en: Now, please let us think!

raw: My esteemed Mr.
en: My dear Mr.

raw: Cruncher, let us think!”
en: Cruncher, let us think!”

raw: Still, Madame Defarge, pursuing her way along the streets, came nearer and nearer.
en: Still, Madame Defarge walked down the streets, coming closer and closer.

raw: “If you were to go before,” said Miss Pross, “and stop the vehicle and horses from coming here, and were to wait somewhere for me; wouldn’t that be best?”
en: “If you went ahead,” Miss Pross said, “and stopped the carriage and horses from coming here, and waited for me somewhere, wouldn't that be best?”

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Cruncher thought it might be best.
en: Cruncher agreed that it might be best.

raw: “Where could you wait for me?” asked Miss Pross.
en: “Where could you wait for me?” asked Miss Pross.

raw: Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Cruncher was so bewildered that he could think of no locality but Temple Bar. Alas!
en: Cruncher was so confused that the only place he could think of was Temple Bar in London.

raw: Temple Bar was hundreds of miles away, and Madame Defarge was drawing very near indeed.
en: But Temple Bar was hundreds of miles away, and Madame Defarge was getting very close indeed.

raw: “By the cathedral door,” said Miss Pross. “Would it be much out of the way, to take me in, near the great cathedral door between the two towers?”
en: “By the cathedral door,” said Miss Pross. “Would it be out of the way to pick me up near the big cathedral door between the two towers?”

raw: “No, miss,” answered Mr.
en: “No, miss,” Mr.

raw: Cruncher.
en: Cruncher answered.

raw: “Then, like the best of men,” said Miss Pross, “go to the posting-house straight, and make that change.”
en: “Then, like the good man you are,” said Miss Pross, “go straight to the carriage station and change the plan.”

raw: “I am doubtful,” said Mr.
en: “I don't know,” said Mr.

raw: Cruncher, hesitating and shaking his head, “about leaving of you, you see.
en: Cruncher, shaking his head. “I'm not sure about leaving you alone.

raw: We don’t know what may happen.”
en: We don't know what might happen.”

raw: “Heaven knows we don’t,” returned Miss Pross, “but have no fear for me.
en: “God knows we don't,” Miss Pross replied, “but don't worry about me.

raw: Take me in at the cathedral, at Three o’Clock, or as near it as you can, and I am sure it will be better than our going from here.
en: Pick me up at the cathedral at three o'clock, or as close to it as you can.

raw: I feel certain of it.
en: I am sure it is better than leaving from this apartment.

raw: There!
en: I'm certain of it.

raw: Bless you, Mr.
en: Go on, and God bless you, Mr.

raw: Cruncher!
en: Cruncher!

raw: Think-not of me, but of the lives that may depend on both of us!”
en: Don't think about me, think about the lives that depend on us!”

raw: This exordium, and Miss Pross’s two hands in quite agonised entreaty clasping his, decided Mr.
en: This speech, along with Miss Pross clutching his hands in desperate begging, convinced Mr.

raw: Cruncher.
en: Cruncher.

raw: With an encouraging nod or two, he immediately went out to alter the arrangements, and left her by herself to follow as she had proposed.
en: With a couple of nods, he immediately went out to change the arrangements, leaving her by herself to follow as planned.

raw: The having originated a precaution which was already in course of execution, was a great relief to Miss Pross.
en: Having come up with a safety plan that was now being carried out was a great relief to Miss Pross.

raw: The necessity of composing her appearance so that it should attract no special notice in the streets, was another relief.
en: The need to fix her appearance so she wouldn't look suspicious in the streets was another distraction.

raw: She looked at her watch, and it was twenty minutes past two.
en: She looked at her watch; it was twenty minutes past two.

raw: She had no time to lose, but must get ready at once.
en: She had no time to lose and had to get ready immediately.

raw: Afraid, in her extreme perturbation, of the loneliness of the deserted rooms, and of half-imagined faces peeping from behind every open door in them, Miss Pross got a basin of cold water and began laving her eyes, which were swollen and red.
en: Terrified in the quiet of the empty rooms, and imagining faces peeping out from behind every open door, Miss Pross got a bowl of cold water and began washing her red, swollen eyes.

raw: Haunted by her feverish apprehensions, she could not bear to have her sight obscured for a minute at a time by the dripping water, but constantly paused and looked round to see that there was no one watching her.
en: Afraid of being snuck up on, she couldn't stand having her eyes closed for even a second by the water, constantly stopping to look around and make sure no one was watching her.

raw: In one of those pauses she recoiled and cried out, for she saw a figure standing in the room.
en: During one of these pauses, she jumped back and screamed, for she saw a figure standing in the room.

raw: The basin fell to the ground broken, and the water flowed to the feet of Madame Defarge.
en: The bowl fell to the floor and shattered, and the water flowed to the feet of Madame Defarge.

raw: By strange stern ways, and through much staining blood, those feet had come to meet that water.
en: By strange, harsh paths and through much spilled blood, those feet had traveled to meet that water.

raw: Madame Defarge looked coldly at her, and said, “The wife of Evrémonde; where is she?”
en: Madame Defarge looked at her coldly and said, “The wife of Evrémonde; where is she?”

raw: It flashed upon Miss Pross’s mind that the doors were all standing open, and would suggest the flight.
en: It flashed in Miss Pross's mind that the open doors would show they had fled.

raw: Her first act was to shut them.
en: Her first reaction was to close them.

raw: There were four in the room, and she shut them all.
en: There were four doors in the room, and she shut them all.

raw: She then placed herself before the door of the chamber which Lucie had occupied.
en: Then she stood directly in front of the door to the bedroom Lucie had used.

raw: Madame Defarge’s dark eyes followed her through this rapid movement, and rested on her when it was finished.
en: Madame Defarge's dark eyes followed her quick movements and stared at her when she stopped.

raw: Miss Pross had nothing beautiful about her; years had not tamed the wildness, or softened the grimness, of her appearance; but, she too was a determined woman in her different way, and she measured Madame Defarge with her eyes, every inch.
en: Miss Pross was not a beautiful woman; age had not softened her sharp, stern looks. But she was just as determined in her own way, and she stared right back at Madame Defarge, sizing her up completely.

raw: “You might, from your appearance, be the wife of Lucifer,” said Miss Pross, in her breathing. “Nevertheless, you shall not get the better of me.
en: “You look like you could be the devil's wife,” Miss Pross muttered under her breath. “But you won't defeat me.

raw: I am an Englishwoman.”
en: I am an Englishwoman.”

raw: Madame Defarge looked at her scornfully, but still with something of Miss Pross’s own perception that they two were at bay.
en: Madame Defarge looked at her with scorn, but both women realized they were trapped in a standoff.

raw: She saw a tight, hard, wiry woman before her, as Mr.
en: She saw a tough, wiry woman in front of her, just as Mr.

raw: Lorry had seen in the same figure a woman with a strong hand, in the years gone by.
en: Years ago, Lorry had seen that this same woman had a strong hand.

raw: She knew full well that Miss Pross was the family’s devoted friend; Miss Pross knew full well that Madame Defarge was the family’s malevolent enemy.
en: She knew very well that Miss Pross was the family's loyal friend; Miss Pross knew very well that Madame Defarge was the family's evil enemy.

raw: “On my way yonder,” said Madame Defarge, with a slight movement of her hand towards the fatal spot, “where they reserve my chair and my knitting for me, I am come to make my compliments to her in passing.
en: “On my way over there,” Madame Defarge said, pointing slightly toward the Guillotine, “where they are saving my chair and knitting, I came to say goodbye to her.

raw: I wish to see her.”
en: I want to see her.”

raw: “I know that your intentions are evil,” said Miss Pross, “and you may depend upon it, I’ll hold my own against them.”
en: “I know you mean to do harm,” said Miss Pross, “and you can be sure I will stand my ground against you.”

raw: Each spoke in her own language; neither understood the other’s words; both were very watchful, and intent to deduce from look and manner, what the unintelligible words meant.
en: Each spoke in her own language, and neither understood the other's words. Both were highly alert, trying to figure out from expressions and gestures what the foreign words meant.

raw: “It will do her no good to keep herself concealed from me at this moment,” said Madame Defarge. “Good patriots will know what that means.
en: “It won't help her to hide from me now,” Madame Defarge said. “Good patriots will know what that hiding means.

raw: Let me see her.
en: Let me see her.

raw: Go tell her that I wish to see her.
en: Go tell her I want to see her.

raw: Do you hear?”
en: Do you hear?”

raw: “If those eyes of yours were bed-winches,” returned Miss Pross, “and I was an English four-poster, they shouldn’t loose a splinter of me.
en: “If your eyes were tools to take apart beds, and I was an English wooden bed, you wouldn't get a single splinter out of me.

raw: No, you wicked foreign woman; I am your match.”
en: No, you wicked foreign woman, I am a match for you.”

raw: Madame Defarge was not likely to follow these idiomatic remarks in detail; but, she so far understood them as to perceive that she was set at naught.
en: Madame Defarge could not follow these English expressions, but she understood enough to see that Miss Pross was refusing to obey her.

raw: “Woman imbecile and pig-like!” said Madame Defarge, frowning. “I take no answer from you.
en: “Foolish, stubborn woman!” Madame Defarge said, frowning. “I won't take no for an answer.

raw: I demand to see her.
en: I demand to see her.

raw: Either tell her that I demand to see her, or stand out of the way of the door and let me go to her!”  This, with an angry explanatory wave of her right arm.
en: Either tell her I am here, or get away from the door and let me in!” She waved her right arm angrily toward the door.

raw: “I little thought,” said Miss Pross, “that I should ever want to understand your nonsensical language; but I would give all I have, except the clothes I wear, to know whether you suspect the truth, or any part of it.”
en: “I never thought I'd want to understand your gibberish language, but I'd give everything I own, except the clothes on my back, to know if you suspect the truth or any part of it.”

raw: Neither of them for a single moment released the other’s eyes.
en: Neither of them broke eye contact for a second.

raw: Madame Defarge had not moved from the spot where she stood when Miss Pross first became aware of her; but, she now advanced one step.
en: Madame Defarge had not moved since entering the room, but now she took a step forward.

raw: “I am a Briton,” said Miss Pross, “I am desperate.
en: “I am a British woman,” said Miss Pross. “I am desperate.

raw: I don’t care an English Twopence for myself.
en: I don't care a penny about my own life.

raw: I know that the longer I keep you here, the greater hope there is for my Ladybird.
en: I know that the longer I keep you here, the more time my darling Lucie has to get away.

raw: I’ll not leave a handful of that dark hair upon your head, if you lay a finger on me!”
en: I won't leave a single strand of hair on your head if you touch me!”

raw: Thus Miss Pross, with a shake of her head and a flash of her eyes between every rapid sentence, and every rapid sentence a whole breath.
en: Miss Pross said this, shaking her head and flashing her eyes with every quick sentence, speaking in rapid breaths.

raw: Thus Miss Pross, who had never struck a blow in her life.
en: This was the same Miss Pross who had never hit anyone in her life.

raw: But, her courage was of that emotional nature that it brought the irrepressible tears into her eyes.
en: But her bravery was so emotional that tears came to her eyes anyway.

raw: This was a courage that Madame Defarge so little comprehended as to mistake for weakness. “Ha, ha!” she laughed, “you poor wretch!
en: Madame Defarge did not understand this kind of courage and mistook it for weakness. “Ha, ha!” she laughed. “You poor wretch!

raw: What are you worth!
en: You are nothing!

raw: I address myself to that Doctor.” Then she raised her voice and called out, “Citizen Doctor!
en: I will speak to the Doctor.” Then she raised her voice and shouted, “Citizen Doctor!

raw: Wife of Evrémonde!
en: Wife of Evrémonde!

raw: Child of Evrémonde!
en: Child of Evrémonde!

raw: Any person but this miserable fool, answer the Citizeness Defarge!”
en: Anyone except this miserable fool, answer Citizenness Defarge!”

raw: Perhaps the following silence, perhaps some latent disclosure in the expression of Miss Pross’s face, perhaps a sudden misgiving apart from either suggestion, whispered to Madame Defarge that they were gone.
en: Perhaps the silence that followed, or something in Miss Pross's face, or a sudden feeling, whispered to Madame Defarge that they were already gone.

raw: Three of the doors she opened swiftly, and looked in.
en: She quickly opened three of the doors and looked inside.

raw: “Those rooms are all in disorder, there has been hurried packing, there are odds and ends upon the ground.
en: “These rooms are a mess; someone packed in a hurry. There are scraps left on the floor.

raw: There is no one in that room behind you!
en: There is no one in that room behind you!

raw: Let me look.”
en: Let me look.”

raw: “Never!” said Miss Pross, who understood the request as perfectly as Madame Defarge understood the answer.
en: “Never!” said Miss Pross, who understood the demand perfectly, just as Madame Defarge understood her refusal.

raw: “If they are not in that room, they are gone, and can be pursued and brought back,” said Madame Defarge to herself.
en: “If they are not in that room, they have fled and can be chased and brought back,” Madame Defarge said to herself.

raw: “As long as you don’t know whether they are in that room or not, you are uncertain what to do,” said Miss Pross to herself; “and you shall not know that, if I can prevent your knowing it; and know that, or not know that, you shall not leave here while I can hold you.”
en: “As long as you don't know if they are in that room, you won't know what to do,” Miss Pross thought to herself. “And I will make sure you never find out. Whether you know it or not, you are not leaving this apartment while I can hold you here.”

raw: “I have been in the streets from the first, nothing has stopped me, I will tear you to pieces, but I will have you from that door,” said Madame Defarge.
en: “I have been fighting in the streets since the start, and nothing has stopped me. I will tear you to pieces to get you away from that door,” Madame Defarge said.

raw: “We are alone at the top of a high house in a solitary courtyard, we are not likely to be heard, and I pray for bodily strength to keep you here, while every minute you are here is worth a hundred thousand guineas to my darling,” said Miss Pross.
en: “We are alone at the top of a tall house in a quiet courtyard where no one will hear us. I pray for the physical strength to keep you here. Every minute you waste is worth a fortune to my darling,” Miss Pross thought.

raw: Madame Defarge made at the door.
en: Madame Defarge lunged for the door.

raw: Miss Pross, on the instinct of the moment, seized her round the waist in both her arms, and held her tight.
en: In that instant, Miss Pross grabbed her around the waist with both arms and held her tight.

raw: It was in vain for Madame Defarge to struggle and to strike; Miss Pross, with the vigorous tenacity of love, always so much stronger than hate, clasped her tight, and even lifted her from the floor in the struggle that they had.
en: It was useless for Madame Defarge to struggle and hit her. Miss Pross, with the fierce strength of love, which is always stronger than hate, held her tightly, even lifting her off the floor as they wrestled.

raw: The two hands of Madame Defarge buffeted and tore her face; but, Miss Pross, with her head down, held her round the waist, and clung to her with more than the hold of a drowning woman.
en: Madame Defarge's hands scratched and beat at her face; but Miss Pross, keeping her head down, held onto her waist like a drowning person clutching for life.

raw: Soon, Madame Defarge’s hands ceased to strike, and felt at her encircled waist. “It is under my arm,” said Miss Pross, in smothered tones, “you shall not draw it.
en: Soon, Madame Defarge stopped hitting and reached down to her waist. “It is under my arm,” Miss Pross said in a muffled voice. “You won't pull that dagger out.

raw: I am stronger than you, I bless Heaven for it.
en: I am stronger than you, thank Heaven.

raw: I hold you till one or other of us faints or dies!”
en: I will hold you until one of us faints or dies!”

raw: Madame Defarge’s hands were at her bosom.
en: Madame Defarge's hands went to her own shirt.

raw: Miss Pross looked up, saw what it was, struck at it, struck out a flash and a crash, and stood alone--blinded with smoke.
en: Miss Pross looked up, saw the pistol, and struck at it. There was a flash and a loud crash, and Miss Pross stood alone, blinded by smoke.

raw: All this was in a second.
en: This all happened in a single second.

raw: As the smoke cleared, leaving an awful stillness, it passed out on the air, like the soul of the furious woman whose body lay lifeless on the ground.
en: As the smoke cleared, leaving a terrifying silence, the smoke drifted out the window, like the soul of the angry woman whose dead body now lay on the floor.

raw: In the first fright and horror of her situation, Miss Pross passed the body as far from it as she could, and ran down the stairs to call for fruitless help.
en: In her initial panic and horror, Miss Pross ran past the body, keeping as far away as possible, and headed down the stairs to call for help.

raw: Happily, she bethought herself of the consequences of what she did, in time to check herself and go back.
en: Fortunately, she realized what would happen if she did that, checked herself, and went back up.

raw: It was dreadful to go in at the door again; but, she did go in, and even went near it, to get the bonnet and other things that she must wear.
en: It was terrifying to enter the room again, but she did, walking close enough to get her hat and coat.

raw: These she put on, out on the staircase, first shutting and locking the door and taking away the key.
en: She put these on out on the staircase, locking the door behind her and taking the key.

raw: She then sat down on the stairs a few moments to breathe and to cry, and then got up and hurried away.
en: She sat on the stairs for a few moments to catch her breath and cry, then got up and hurried away.

raw: By good fortune she had a veil on her bonnet, or she could hardly have gone along the streets without being stopped.
en: Luckily she had a veil on her hat, or she would have been stopped in the streets immediately.

raw: By good fortune, too, she was naturally so peculiar in appearance as not to show disfigurement like any other woman.
en: Luckily, too, her unusual appearance made her injuries less obvious than they would be on anyone else.

raw: She needed both advantages, for the marks of gripping fingers were deep in her face, and her hair was torn, and her dress (hastily composed with unsteady hands) was clutched and dragged a hundred ways.
en: She needed both advantages, because deep finger marks were bruised onto her face, her hair was torn, and her dress, which she had tried to fix with shaking hands, was ripped and messy.

raw: In crossing the bridge, she dropped the door key in the river.
en: As she crossed the bridge, she threw the door key into the river.

raw: Arriving at the cathedral some few minutes before her escort, and waiting there, she thought, what if the key were already taken in a net, what if it were identified, what if the door were opened and the remains discovered, what if she were stopped at the gate, sent to prison, and charged with murder!
en: She arrived at the cathedral a few minutes before Jerry and waited there, worrying: what if the key was caught in a fishing net? What if it was identified? What if the apartment door was opened and the body discovered? What if she was stopped at the city gates, sent to prison, and charged with murder?

raw: In the midst of these fluttering thoughts, the escort appeared, took her in, and took her away.
en: In the middle of these panicked thoughts, Jerry arrived with the carriage, picked her up, and drove away.

raw: “Is there any noise in the streets?” she asked him.
en: “Is there any noise in the streets?” she asked him.

raw: “The usual noises,” Mr.
en: “Just the usual noises,” Mr.

raw: Cruncher replied; and looked surprised by the question and by her aspect.
en: Cruncher replied, looking surprised by her question and her messy appearance.

raw: “I don’t hear you,” said Miss Pross. “What do you say?” It was in vain for Mr.
en: “I can't hear you,” said Miss Pross. “What did you say?” It was useless for Mr.

raw: Cruncher to repeat what he said; Miss Pross could not hear him. “So I’ll nod my head,” thought Mr.
en: Cruncher to repeat himself; Miss Pross could not hear a word. “So I'll just nod my head,” Mr.

raw: Cruncher, amazed, “at all events she’ll see that.” And she did.
en: Cruncher thought in surprise, “at least she will see that.” And she did.

raw: “Is there any noise in the streets now?” asked Miss Pross again, presently.
en: “Is there any noise in the streets now?” Miss Pross asked again soon.

raw: Again Mr.
en: Mr.

raw: Cruncher nodded his head.
en: Cruncher nodded again.

raw: “I don’t hear it.”
en: “I don't hear anything.”

raw: “Gone deaf in an hour?” said Mr.
en: “Deaf in just an hour?” Mr.

raw: Cruncher, ruminating, with his mind much disturbed; “wot’s come to her?”
en: Cruncher thought, deeply worried. “What happened to her?”

raw: “I feel,” said Miss Pross, “as if there had been a flash and a crash, and that crash was the last thing I should ever hear in this life.”
en: “I feel,” said Miss Pross, “as if there was a flash and a crash, and that crash was the very last thing I will ever hear in this life.”

raw: “Blest if she ain’t in a queer condition!” said Mr.
en: “She is in a very strange state!” Mr.

raw: Cruncher, more and more disturbed. “Wot can she have been a takin’, to keep her courage up?
en: Cruncher said, becoming more worried. “What did she drink to keep her courage up?

raw: Hark!
en: Listen!

raw: There’s the roll of them dreadful carts!
en: There is the rumble of those terrible carts!

raw: You can hear that, miss?”
en: Surely you can hear that, miss?”

raw: “I can hear,” said Miss Pross, seeing that he spoke to her, “nothing.
en: “I can hear nothing,” said Miss Pross, seeing him speak. “Oh, my good man, first there was a great crash, and then a great silence.

raw: O, my good man, there was first a great crash, and then a great stillness, and that stillness seems to be fixed and unchangeable, never to be broken any more as long as my life lasts.”
en: Oh, my good man, first there was a loud crash, and then a deep silence. That silence seems permanent, never to be broken again for as long as I live.

raw: “If she don’t hear the roll of those dreadful carts, now very nigh their journey’s end,” said Mr.
en: “If she can't hear the rumble of those death carts, which are very close to their destination now,” Mr.

raw: Cruncher, glancing over his shoulder, “it’s my opinion that indeed she never will hear anything else in this world.”
en: Cruncher said, looking over his shoulder, “I don't think she will ever hear anything in this world again.”

raw: And indeed she never did.
en: And indeed, she never did.
